item.title: 28 Introduction
item.description:
SECTION VII

CHAPTER XXVIII [[MĪMĀŃSA AND DHARMASĀSTRA|MĪMĀṀSĀ AND DHARMAŚĀSTRA]]

[[P1152]]The Yājñavalkya-smrti provides that there are fourteen sources of vidyās ([[knowledge )|knowledge)]] and of [[Dharma, 1863|Dharma]],1 viz. Purāṇa, Nyāya, [[Mimāṁsā,|Mīmāṁsā,]] Dharmaśāstra, [[Angas|Aṅgas]] (six) and the Vedas (four). A similar verse is quoted by some as Manu’s, but it is not found in the extant [[Manusmrti.|Manusmṛti.]] It is therefore necessary to consider the origin and meaning of the word [[Mimāmsā,|Mīmāṁsā,]] to set out the principal doctrines of that [[Sāstra,|Śāstra,]] to mention the important rules of interpretation and the maxims of the [[Mimāṁsā|Mīmāṁsā]] in their application to topics of Dharmaśāstra and to refer to some of the important works of that Śāstra together with their approximate dates.

item.title: 29 Doctrines of Mīmāṃsā
item.description:
[[P1202]]CHAPTER XXIX

Some Fundamental Doctrines of [[Purvamimāmsā|Pūrvamīmāṁsā]]

Some of the characteristic fundamental doctrines of the [[Pūrvamimāṁsā|Pūrvamīmāṁsā]] will now be set out with some references and a few [[renarks|remarks]] as to some of them, the views of [[Prabhakara|Prabhākara]] and his followers being also rarely referred [[to|to.]]

(1) Veda is eternal, self-existent, not composed by any author, human or divine, and is infallible. This is the core of the [[P, M,|P. M.]] system. Vide P. M. S. [[1. 1.|I. 1.]] 27-32 and [[Sabara|Śabara]] on [[1, 1.|I. 1.]] 5 (p. 53) and [[ślokavārtika|Ślokavārtika]] ([[Vākyādhikarana,|Vākyādhikaraṇa,]] [[verges 1953|verses]] 1 [[366 368|366-368]]). The argument briefly is; Veda is learnt at present and [[. was|was]] studied in [[tbe|the]] past also by students from teachers, that there is no evidence about the person who first composed it or who first studied it. If it be argued that such a reasoning may be put forward as regards the [[Mahabharata|Mahābhārata]], the reply is that people know that Vyāsa is the author of it. Similarly, the passages in [[Smrtis|Smṛtis]] and Purāṇas that [[Prajapati|Prajāpati]] created the Veda are merely [[artharadas|arthavādas]] ([[laudatory )|laudatory)]] not based on any evidence or perception and are meant only to convey the absolute [[autho ritativeness|authoritativeness]] of the Veda. If the connection between word and [[. songe|sense]] is eternal and not brought about by any person, the same reasoning holds good as to the Veda. This view is opposed to the view of the Naiyāyikas who hold that God is the author of the [[Voda|Veda]] or the interpretation of V. S. item.title: 30 Mīmāṃsā Priniciples and Dharmaśāstra
item.description:
CHAPTER XXX On [[Mināmsā|Mīmāṁsā]] principles and rules of interpretation in relation to [[Dharmasastra|Dharmaśāstra]]

[[P1283]]The [[Pārvamimamas ayolyed|Pūrvamīmāṁsā evolved]] a method of its own and a set of principles for the interpretation of Vedic texts. It is now time to [[get|set]] down and explain some of these principles and [[rulea|rules]] and point out how they have been employed by [[Dharmasastra|Dharmaśāstra]] writers for solving their own difficulties.

The [[Mimārsā|Mīmāṁsā]] principles and rules of interpretation fall into several groups. There are rules that are concerned only with the details of Vedic [[saorifices|sacrifices]] and their inter-relations. The most important rule in this field is this that only Vidhis properly so called have absolute authority and binding force, while what are called arthavādas have authority in so far only as they form one syntactical whole with the vidhis and as they are meant to praise the vidhis. (P. M. [[8.|S.]] I. [[2.7).|2. 7).]] Vidhis and Arthavādas are not discussed consecutively, but they are scattered over the several chapters of the P. M. S. For example, arthavādas are first dealt with in I. [[%.|2.]] 1-18 (the [[arthavadādhi karaña|arthavādādhikaraṇa]]), but in many other places there is a discussion about arthavādas as in III. 4. 1-9, [[II, 4, 10,|III. 4. 10,]] III. 4. 11, IV. 3. 1-3, VI. 7. 26–30, X. 8. 5, X. 8. 7 and 8.
